SOURCE: Self-Challenging Language Model Agents. Yifei Zhou, Sergey Levine, Jason Weston, Xian Li, Sainbayar Sukhbaatar (UC Berkeley, FAIR at Meta). arXiv:2506.01716v1, 2 Jun 2025, labelled "Preprint".
COVERAGE: All 25 pages read (extraction of 92,349 chars, 1,473 lines; /tmp/zhou.txt). Main text, appendices A-I, tables and hyperparameters were read in full. The prompt-listing pages (Figures 9-14 read, Figures 15-20 only grepped by caption) were skimmed. References were skimmed for origins.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Self-improvement: Llama-3.1-8B training on its own Code-as-Task (CaT) tasks roughly doubles average success.
  number: Pass@1 12.0 -> 23.5 average; Pass@4 27.9 -> 41.3
  setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is both challenger and executor. 800 synthetic tasks and 12k offline rollouts per environment, trained by rejection fine-tuning. Evaluated on real test tasks from M3ToolEval (Calculation, Web Browsing) and Tau-Bench (Retail, Airline). Pass@1 averaged over 4 trials; pass@4 is computed from the same four trials.
  quote: "SCA training is able to double the success rate from 12.0% to 23.5%, outperforming the prior state-of-the-art self-improvement method for LLM agents by a wide margin."
  where: p.2 (intro); Table 1, p.6
- Self-improvement versus the PAE baseline (Proposer-Agent-Evaluator: an LLM proposes tasks and the same LLM judges success). PAE averages 12.9 against 23.5 for SCA.
  number: +11.5 over base and +10.6 over PAE in Pass@1. Per environment, SCA/PAE Pass@1: Calc 31.8/27.6, Web 44.9/14.0, Retail 13.0/9.8, Airline 4.2/0.0.
  setup: as above.
  quote: "with an average of +11.5% gain compared to the base model and a +10.6% advantage compared to PAE in terms of Pass@1."
  where: p.7; Table 1
- PAE self-improvement can hurt in partially observable settings.
  number: Airline Pass@4 falls 10 -> 0 under PAE
  quote: "the autonomously proposed tasks from PAE in Airline actually result in a -10% drop to 0% Pass@4."
  where: p.7
- Distillation: a 70B teacher's trajectories on synthetic tasks lift the 8B student.
  number: average Pass@1 12.0 -> 32.2 (SCA); PAE gets 30.1
  setup: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct samples trajectories, SFT on all trajectories (successful and failed). Same 800 tasks and 12k rollouts.
  quote: "we are able to improve the student model Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [34] by 20.2% in terms of absolute average success rate across all 4 environments without any existing tasks."
  where: p.2; Table 1
- Failed teacher trajectories help distillation.
  number: Pass@1 average 32.2 (all trajectories) against 27.8 (successes only); Pass@4 56.8 against 48.1
  quote: "distillation on both successful and unsuccessful trajectories tend to yield better results compared to successful trajectories only across the board."
  where: Table 3, p.15
- Each CaT component filters out bad tasks, but the pass rate of the challenger falls sharply. The verification function must be checked against both a solution and failure cases.
  number: Share of generated tasks passing all filters: verification only 47.7%, +solution 9.5%, full CaT 5.2%
  setup: Llama-3.1-8B challenger in Retail. 50 passing tasks per variant, with one rollout trajectory per task hand-labelled by an author into TP/TN/FP/FN (the text later says 200 trajectories per variant, 8 human-hours).
  quote: "After filtering, 47.7% of tasks remain with this variant." / "The percentage of passing tasks for this variant is 9.5%." / "The percentage of passing tasks for full CaT is 5.2%."
  where: p.7-8; Fig 4
- A solution-only check makes verifiers too lenient. Adding failure cases removes false positives.
  number: none (Fig 4 bar heights not extractable)
  quote: "the filtering mechanism based on the example solution passing verification functions tends to amplify this distribution. Fortunately, we can apply a simple fix by adding another filtering mechanism based on failure cases to completely remove FP in CaT."
  where: p.8
- False negatives remain even with full CaT. Incomplete instructions are the main cause, for example "Help me return one of my latest orders".
  number: none
  quote: "The main failure mode of FN in CaT is incomplete instructions where the instruction does not contain all necessary information to complete the task."
  where: p.8
- Filtering narrows the task distribution for a weak challenger but not a strong one.
  number: pass rate 5.3% for 8B, 34.4% for 70B (Fig 5 labels)
  setup: Retail; difficulty is measured as example-solution length.
  quote: "CaT filtering can result in a less diverse task distribution for the less capable Llama-3.1-8B but preserves the original task distribution for the stronger Llama-3.1-70B model."
  where: Fig 5, p.9. The text says 5.2% for the full-CaT pass rate in Fig 4 and 5.3% in Fig 5, so the two are slightly inconsistent.
- Online RL beats offline RL on the same tasks but is unstable.
  number: offline (rejection fine-tuning, DPO) 20.3 -> 31.8 Pass@1; online (PPO, GRPO) reaches 43.2
  setup: M3ToolEval Calculation only.
  quote: "While offline methods such as Rejection Fine-Tuning and DPO can already achieve significant self-improvements from 20.3% to 31.8% Pass@1 success rate, online RL on the same tasks can push the performance to another level of 43.2% Pass@1."
  where: p.7; Fig 3
  related quote: "the performance of GRPO suddenly drops to 0% at the end of training when it is not tuned carefully."
- Scale the number of tasks, not the trajectories per task.
  number: 200 tasks slightly degrades out-of-distribution (OOD) test results; 400 tasks gives marginal gains; 800 tasks improves steadily
  setup: M3ToolEval Calculation. Training success keeps rising with more rollouts on every set size.
  quote: "training on 200 tasks even slightly degrades the test set Pass@1 and Pass@4 performance, and training on 400 tasks only leads to marginal improvements."
  where: p.9; Fig 6
- Loss reduces to rejection fine-tuning with a binary reward (REINFORCE on 0/1 outcome reward).
  quote: "this RL optimization objective is essentially equivalent to performing supervised finetuning (SFT) on successful trajectories (i.e. R̂ĉ(sT , aT ) = 1) only, i.e. Rejection Fine-Tuning."
  number: none
  where: p.5, Eq. 2
- Synthetic tasks fall short of oracle (hand-seeded) tasks.
  number: none stated; the gap is shown only in Fig 7 (PPO, 800 tasks each)
  quote: "there remains a sub-optimality gap compared to using oracle tasks"
  where: p.15
- Gains are environment-specific; joint training does not help.
  number: cross-task average Pass@1 23.0 against 23.5 separate; Pass@4 39.8 against 41.3
  quote: "we found marginal improvements, or even worse performances, of training a joint model on the data from all environments."
  where: Table 2, p.14-15
- Verifier hygiene: 40% of the Airline test tasks counted as successful with no action taken, so the authors removed them.
  number: 40%
  quote: "We noticed 40% of the tasks in Airline are considered successful when no actions are taken so we removed them from our experiments to reduce noise."
  where: App. A, p.14
- The automatic checker returns its error traceback to the challenger, so it can revise the task.
  quote: "If the automatic checker fails, it will return its error traceback to the task challenger to revise the task."
  number: none
  where: App. A
- Compute (8xA100 80G, hours):
  number: challenge generation 8 (Calc/Web) or 32 (Retail/Airline); rollouts 24; rejection fine-tuning 3; evaluation 0.5-2
  quote: "We find the main bottlenecks to be challenges generation and rollouts generations"
  where: App. F, Table 4

LIMITS
- Authors concede a non-trivial false-negative rate from ambiguity and missing information (Limitations, p.9).
- Authors concede the SCA-versus-oracle gap and that agents "mostly improve its environment-specific skills instead of overall agentic capabilities" (Limitations, p.9).
- Conclusion calls it "a preliminary step".
- Only Llama-3.1-8B was trained. Self-improvement used the 8B as its own user simulator in Tau-Bench, but evaluation used GPT-4o as the simulator.
- Absolute scores stay low: Airline is 4.2 Pass@1 after self-improvement. The 8B also stays below the zero-shot 70B and GPT-4o on most environments.
- Pass@1 is averaged over only 4 trials. No variance or seeds are reported.
- The human-annotation sample is small (50 tasks per variant; one author labels).
- Fig 4 bar values were not extracted, so FP/FN percentages are unquoted.
- The paper does not run an iterative multi-round loop. It is one generate, filter, rollout, train pass. The "flywheel" is future work.
- Dated: Llama-3.1 era, 2025. The concurrent Absolute Zero (Zhao et al.) is cited as related.
- The abstract says "over a two-fold improvement"; the conclusion states "an average relative success rate improvement of 95.8%". Treat the two-fold claim as approximate, since 95.8% relative is just under 2x.

BUILDS ON
- Asymmetric self-play (Sukhbaatar et al. 2018 [33]; OpenAI et al. 2021 [21]).
- PAE (Zhou et al. 2024 [51]) as the baseline and predecessor.
- Self-Instruct (Wang et al. 2023 [38]).
- Self-Rewarding LMs (Yuan et al. 2024 [47]).
- M3ToolEval / CodeAct (Wang et al. 2024 [37]) and tau-bench (Yao et al. 2024 [46]).
- REINFORCE (Williams), DPO (Rafailov et al.), PPO (Schulman et al. 2017), GRPO (Shao et al. 2024).
- Code-as-policies (Liang et al. 2023).
- Autonomous evaluators (Pan et al. 2024 [23]).

CODE
Verifier plus solution plus failure-case format (Fig 9, p.18):
```
<evaluation_function>
def evaluate():
success = True
order = get_order_details("#W3977493")
success = success and (order["status] == "exchange requested")
...
return success
</evaluation_function>
<solution>exchange_delivered_order_items(...)</solution>
<failure_case>#an example edge-case solution that should not pass the evaluation function ...</failure_case>
```
The challenger prompt requires at least 3 failure cases ("You should write at least 3 failure cases.") and tells the challenger to run its solution and verifier before answering ("TRY RUNNING THE SOLUTION AND EVALUATION FUNCTION FIRST..."). Fig 2 caption: "Automatic filtering is applied to CaTs to keep only valid tasks where the example solution can pass the verification function and the failure cases cannot." The checker has three conditions (App. A): code runs, solution passes, failure cases fail. Tasks are reset to the same hidden environment state per attempt.
Hyperparameters (Table 5): rejection fine-tuning lr 1e-5, batch 8, 6 epochs; PPO/GRPO lr 1e-6, batch 256, clip 0.1, KL coef 0.001.

FIGURES
- Fig 1, p.2: challenger/executor loop with verifier giving a 0/1 reward. Shows the whole architecture.
- Fig 2, p.4: a CaT example with the assert True/assert False checks. Shows the filter logic.
- Fig 3, p.7: RL algorithm comparison (rejection fine-tuning, DPO, PPO, GRPO) against number of trajectories.
- Fig 4, p.8: TP/TN/FP/FN per variant, with pass rates in the labels (100%, 47.7%, 9.5%, 5.2%).
- Fig 5, p.9: task-difficulty distribution before and after filtering, 8B against 70B.
- Fig 6, p.9: task count against trajectories per task, train against OOD test.
- Fig 7, p.15: SCA tasks against oracle tasks.
- Figs 15-19, App. H: a full CaT example, and the failure-mode example for each variant.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The pypdf run printed fontTools warnings, which are harmless. Tables and figure axes extracted as flat numbers, so bar heights in Fig 4 and the curves in Figs 3, 5, 6 and 7 are not available as numbers. In the Figure 9 prompt text, quotes and indentation were lost in extraction (for example `order["status]`), and the prompt example fails its own filter (the "wrong" `new_item_ids` ids do not match the `7533802601` example), which I report as printed. The Fig 10 example solution has a date inconsistency (HAT172 on 2024-05-24 against the verifier's 2024-05-25), as printed. Text extract saved at /tmp/zhou.txt.
